newsitem.title: HUNGARY: New EU members must accept sugar rules -Brussels.
newsitem.headline: New EU members must accept sugar rules -Brussels.

text.p: Sugar industries of countries seeking European Union membership will have to accept the EU's existing sugar regulations, an official said on Tuesday.
"They will have to accept the policy as it stands," Ejner Stendevad, head of sugar in the European Commission's Directorate General for Agriculture, told a news conference.
He was speaking after a two-day conference in Budapest on the sugar industry in central and eastern Europe, the participants of which have all expressed their intention to join the EU.
Stendevad said that EU hopefuls would be better off copying the EU's sugar legislation than trying to negotiate special deals.
"We have seen in earlier accessions that those who have adapted to our system, had advantages and had less teething problems," he said.
He added that sugar legislation closer to EU standards would encourage foreign companies to invest in the sugar industry of countries which needed investment.
"The sugar industry is very capital-demanding and in many countries...it might be the question of foreign investment," Stendevad said, adding that foreign investors expected stability.
He added, however, that Hungary's sugar industry could in many respects match the EU's sugar regulations in time.
"Hungary might be ready to enter our framework when the politicians are ready," Stendevad said.
But Hungary might have its own problems with sugar regulations as they were supposed to form part of a national agricultural strategy yet to be formulated.

"We hope that the framework (on sugar) will be in place by October," said Karoly Fabian, president of the Hungarian Sugar Producers' Association, adding that it might be ready before the whole of the strategy was devised.

Sugar industry sources said in early January that after satisfying domestic demand of some 450,000 tonnes this year, Hungary would have about 120,000 tonnes of sugar to export from 1996/97 production.
But high domestic production costs and the absecne of export subsidies on sugar meant Hungarian sugar could only be exported to nearby countries such as Yugoslavia or Romania.
Sugar production costs in Hungary were between 92,000 and 97,000 forints per tonne.

Austria's Agrana International AG controls over 50 percent of Hungary's refining capacity, with France's Eridania Beghin-Say and the UK's Tate & Lyle also holding considerable stakes in Hungarian refineries.
